1:
Ellicott measures the gap. Perhaps a year had passed, and much had happened to discredit the prophet: the child was born but the northern kingdom still stood, multitudes had gone captive to Damascus, the Edomites were harassing the frontier, and the loss of Elath had cut the Red Sea trade. To a weak king the prospect looked darker than ever and Assyria the only hope. The question was whether the prophet should recant; the answer was that he must repeat everything more definitely than before. Gill and Calvin note that it confirms rather than extends the last. Clarke, mapping the chapter, remarks on the prophet constant practice of joining temporal deliverances to spiritual ones.

What he is told to write on divides the voices. Henry and Wesley picture a great roll or volume, large because the matter was. Ellicott prefers a large tablet, the noun being the one used earlier for mirrors: prophetic writings went on papyrus to disciples, private messages on small waxed tablets written with an iron stylus. Here the tablet is large and the writing not a scribe fine point but a common workman pen, the kind used for sign-boards, to catch a passer-by eye. Calvin argues from the other end: small writing is obscure, and a man pen means a man of ordinary rank, so not even the uneducated should fail to read it. Four words carried more force than a long discourse, since anyone could take four words home; and he thinks it was fixed to the temple gates so the phrase might be repeated like a proverb. Henry agrees that those who write for men should not covet the pen of angels.

Calvin blocks a reading he finds attractive but wrong. Because the previous chapter spoke of the coming of Christ, many explain this name of him too, as one who came to spoil the strong; he calls the ingenuity pleasing enough but says it cannot harmonize with the text.

The witnesses raise a problem. Ellicott supposes men of high position, probably among those who had pressed for the alliance. Of Uriah it is known that he gave the king an altar copied from one at Damascus; Henry says he is mentioned in that history for none of his good deeds, though no exception lay against him here. Calvin is blunter: one of the two was an ungodly apostate who defended unlawful worship to flatter his king, and those who make him a different man argue weakly from the word faithful, since the prophet looked not at the man but at the office, which made his testimony unobjectionable. Of Zechariah nothing certain is known; Ellicott canvasses the conjecture that he wrote part of the book bearing a later prophet name, and thinks him likelier the grandfather of Hezekiah. Both men may have been chosen for what their names mean, that the Lord is my light and that the Lord will remember.

On the birth Calvin stands alone. He judges that what follows came in a vision, sealing the earlier prediction, since it is improbable the name was ever given to a man. He will not argue hard against a literal reading and grants no absurdity in a real son, but calls the wife a prophetess because in the vision she sustained a public character. Gill and Wesley take the marriage as real and the title as courtesy, a prophet wife rather than one who prophesied. Ellicott allows the courtesy sense but notes that elsewhere the word implies real prophetic gift, and suggests the two were drawn together by shared counsels, unlike the celibacy of Jeremiah, the miserable marriage of Hosea, or the bereavement of Ezekiel. Keil and Delitzsch put the transition best: the lifeless table gave place to a more eloquent and living one. Henry makes the child a walking memorandum, the elder brother name having spoken mercy and this one, mercy slighted, judgment.
4:
The time limit set by the child is read two ways. Gill, Ellicott and Wesley take it of the boy just named, the first words a child learns being the measure. Ellicott supposes the witnesses were summoned to the circumcision and naming, so the name at which Jerusalem had gazed was fastened on a newborn; he makes the limit a year. Wesley prefers two years, and reconciles the two signs by noting that knowing to refuse the evil takes longer than distinguishing parents. Calvin dissents: he understands not the prophet own son but all children born about that time, so the two kingdoms fall before that generation is grown.

Clarke supplies a variant and a fulfilment. One manuscript and the Vulgate read his father and his mother for my father and my mother; and the thing was done within three years, when Tiglath-pileser took Damascus, carried its people to Kir, killed Rezin, and swept away the Reubenites, the Gadites and half of Manasseh. Ellicott splits the fulfilment, the region beyond Jordan and Damascus falling to that king while Samaria fell to Sargon. Calvin notes that the words, addressed to a king who believes nothing, are spoken less to him than to the godly, to show that such wickedness does not shut the door of mercy.

Keil and Delitzsch mark the new heading as governing everything to the end of the section, and observe that all of it finishes in consolation; but consolation presupposes a need of it, so even here the prophet begins with a threat. They derive the name of the brook from a root meaning to send forth, and Gill, identifying it with Siloam, notes the same sense, reporting from Jarchi that the fountain bore two names.

Who is meant by this people is the first real crux. Wesley takes it of Israel, who rejoiced not only in their own king but in the help of so powerful an ally. Ellicott grants that the phrase might grammatically point to Judah, and follows that into politics: the tyranny of Ahaz had made him so unpopular that his subjects may have welcomed the invaders, so he sought the alliance against his own people as much as against the confederates, like a Ferdinand of Naples falling back on Austria against Garibaldi and Victor Emmanuel. What line, he asks, was the prophet to take between a bad king and subjects ready to sell their independence? He takes neither side and warns each, finding it monstrous that Judah should copy the confederates. Calvin rejects a narrow reading, that the rebuke falls only on men who wanted a change of ruler, as a sick man hopes for relief from a change of place. His sense takes in every rank, since almost the whole nation was corrupted; and the offence he names is envy, the people distrusting their small numbers and longing for the forces of the kingdom of Israel.

Clarke makes the two waters a study in contrast. The gentle brook, a small fountain feeding a pool for the inhabitants, is an apt emblem of a house much reduced in strength yet supported by the blessing of God, set against the impetuous river he takes as the image of an empire coming down like a flood on the apostates of both kingdoms. He then reaches for two Roman poets who used rivers the same way, one complaining that the Orontes had long discharged itself into the Tiber, the other saying the Euphrates now flowed more humbly; and judges their single figures unable to contend with the prophet paired one. Ellicott builds the contrast from geography, setting the little stream that rises between the two hills of the city against the Nile, the Euphrates and the Tigris, on which the capitals of great empires stood. Wesley reduces it to what the enemies saw, the munitions and strength of the Jews, which they derided.
7:
Every voice identifies the river as the Euphrates and the Assyrian power. Wesley notes it is called the river for its greatness; Gill sets it against the little brook as the stream that ran by Babylon. Ellicott makes the symbolism precise: the river stands for the monarchy, as the brook had stood for Judah, and for the armies pouring down in flood; the channels and banks mark the course the invasion was meant to take, the overflow its spilling into Judah. The difference in outcome matters to him, since the confederate kingdoms are wholly submerged while Judah is reached only to the neck.

Calvin turns the image into an argument about what the people wanted. Suppose a small nation with a mean king envied powerful neighbours under an illustrious one, and said how delightful it would be to serve so prosperous a king, an emperor or the kings of France. Would God not justly punish such a desire? The more powerful kings are, the more grievously they oppress; there is nothing they will not attempt, and in proportion to their strength they indulge with less restraint. So the threat answers the wish: I will show you what a powerful king is. The Assyrians called in for help were the ones who destroyed them, the just punishment of their distrust. He draws a rule and guards it. The Church is almost always destitute of human aid, lest being too largely furnished it be dazzled by its wealth and forget God, so the gentle waters should be valued above the great rivers of the nations. But he will not be made to say more than he means: the prophet condemns not human aid but the fear that throws us into distrust; if we have such help, we are at liberty to use it.

Clarke reports from Kimchi that Jerusalem is the head of the body, so that as a man with water at his neck is near drowning, the country was overflowed and the capital in danger; and the Chaldee renders reaching to the neck as reaching to Jerusalem. Calvin builds it from a man wading in and sinking gradually, the neck being the metropolis. Wesley fixes the moment, when Sennacherib took the fenced cities and sent his army against the capital. Gill adds that the power sent for as a helper became the distress.

Ellicott admires the next figure as a metaphor inside a metaphor, quite after this prophet manner: the armies are a river in flood, and the water spreading either side of the main stream is like the wings of a great bird stooping on its prey. Wesley reads them plainly, as the wings of an army.

The address at the close divides the voices. Ellicott takes it of the earthly child, whose name the prophet has not forgotten, and says the land belongs to one who is in very deed God with us; he points to a psalm which is either this prophecy turned into a hymn or the hymn that was its germ, the parallel proving the two contemporary. Calvin has no doubt the name means Christ, and asks why the prophet addresses him instead of calling the country the holy land of God. One answer would sharpen the disgrace, a country having the Mediator as guardian yet wasted by a heathen king; but Calvin prefers consolation, a remnant of hope for good men whose courage might fail, meaning the desolation will not prevent the coming of the Redeemer, and the land still belongs to God and not to men. He calls the sudden turn to direct address emphatic, meant to set a limit to the calamities. Wesley reaches the same end another way, taking the land as Judah because the Messiah was to be born there, and finding the assurance that God would distinguish the kingdoms, Israel ceasing to be a people while Judah was restored.
9:
Keil and Delitzsch catch the turn: the imploring look at Immanuel does not go unanswered, and what was almost a silent prayer changes at once into the jubilate of holy defiance. Calvin describes the same movement as a change of vantage. The prophet stands as on a watch-tower, seeing the distressed people below and the enemy exulting over them; refreshed by the sight of Christ he forgets his distresses and taunts the enemies as if he had vanquished them.

The opening verb is disputed three ways. The received reading gives a summons to associate, taken by Gill and Wesley of the confederate powers. Clarke finds the present text subject to many difficulties and follows the Septuagint, reading a call to know this, parallel with the give ear of the next line, and notes that Archbishop Secker approves the change; he also admires its paraphrase, that when they have strengthened themselves they shall be broken, and strengthening themselves again shall be broken again. Keil and Delitzsch reject the association sense the Targum adopts and take the root in its other meaning, so the nations are told to exasperate themselves and go to pieces. Calvin knows both derivations, thinks the associate sense agrees better with the argument, then prefers a metaphor of pressing together, illustrated from his own vernacular: draw close to one another as if you were a dense mass.

Who is addressed matters as much as how. Gill and Wesley keep the confederates. Ellicott would render peoples in the plural, a challenge to all the earth, near and far, since no plan against the divine kingdom, of which the house of David was then the representative, shall prosper. Calvin asks why peoples, when only one power was to lay waste the country, and gives two answers: the invading army was itself made of many nations, or the prophet looks past this stroke to the incessant contests still to come, taking in Syrians and Egyptians and every enemy of the Church.

Henry stages the passage as a taunt in two halves. First he grants the enemy everything: they associate, gird and gird again, call councils of war, and are confident the matter will be done at a word speaking; and he notes how much policy the enemies of the Church bring to their designs, and what pains they take to roll a stone that will certainly return upon them. Then the reversal, sharpened into a sentence: not only shall their attempts be ruined, but their attempts shall be their ruin. Their counsels come to nothing because there is no wisdom nor counsel against the Lord. This, he says, is how the daughter of Zion despises them.

Calvin separates the two verses by the kind of strength each answers. The first deals with forces, the second with counsel, and he explains why: we often despise powerful enemies because they lack judgment and are guided by blind violence rather than reason, so it must be said that their craftiness too will fail. The passage then serves as a shield against adversaries who excel either in forces and rank or in wisdom and invention. But he attaches a warning to the ground of confidence. Wicked men also boast that God is with them and grow insolent on it, and their glorying is idle; the valour of the godly rests on the word and proceeds from true faith, and only then is the boast not made in vain. He adds that the majesty of God is not by itself sufficient to support us, so the prophet contemplates him in the person of the Mediator. Keil and Delitzsch make the same point: it is Immanuel whom believers hold fast as their refuge in the approaching judgment, and God in him, and not any human support whatever. Wesley notes only that the threat is doubled for greater assurance and for the comfort of the people of God.
11:
The strong hand is read as pressure of one kind or another. Gill notes that the Targum and the Jewish interpreters take it of prophecy, but offers the alternative that God took the prophet by the hand, as parents do with children. Clarke prefers that on manuscript grounds, since eleven copies collated by Kennicott, thirty-four of De Rossi, and the readings of Symmachus, the Syriac and the Vulgate support taking me by the hand; though he allows a strong hand may stand, meaning a powerful prophetic influence. Wesley calls it a more than ordinary inspiration, Ellicott an anthropomorphism for unusual intensity. Calvin thinks the commentators have missed the figure. It is a teacher whose words have not taken effect seizing the hand of the child to compel obedience; the servants of God are sometimes ready to throw everything away, believing they labour to no purpose, and are held to their duty by force.

Calvin sets the passage against two temptations, an external one from open enemies and an internal one, far worse, in which a chosen people relied on man rather than God. The mechanism he most fears is imitation: when others go before us we treat their example as a licence, and once a practice is universal what is plainly wrong hides under the cloak of public opinion, as though the will of the people could authorise its corruptions.

What the people must not say divides the voices four ways. Gill takes it of the alliance with Assyria, and notes the Targum reading of rebellion against the king. Calvin agrees, taking the word of the league many unbelievers were eager to contract rather than of the enemy league. Ellicott lists three possibilities, the confederacy of the northern powers, the cry of conspiracy raised by the pro-Assyrian party against the prophet, and the emendation making the word a holy thing; he judges the second most in harmony with the sequence. Clarke goes furthest. He finds both reading and sense doubtful, notes that the Septuagint read a word meaning hard while the Syriac and Chaldee render rebellion, and objects that none yields a clear sense nor explains how saying such a thing would be walking in the way of this people. He therefore adopts the conjecture of Archbishop Secker, offered with great diffidence and almost withdrawn for want of authority, that the word be read as holy: call not their idols holy, nor fear what they fear, but look to the Lord as your Holy One He urges that the two words differ by transposing letters hardly distinguishable in many copies, and that the reading makes the sentence run in harmony.

Clarke keeps the gloss consistent, taking the next word for the thing feared. Wesley makes it the dread that without Assyrian help they perish. Calvin observes that the same alarm faced godly and ungodly alike but was not met alike, and says fear is not forbidden, only the terror that swallows the ungodly up.

To sanctify the Lord is the remedy. Ellicott hears an appeal to the earlier vision, asking whether the disciples had entered into its thrice-repeated holy. Gill names the one to be sanctified as Immanuel; Wesley makes it a matter of trusting the promises. Calvin defines it as exalting his power so as to remember that he governs the world; hence his sharpest sentence, that God is in some measure robbed of his holiness when we do not go straight to him in perplexity, no higher affront being possible than to give way to fear as though he were not above his creatures. If we are not convinced that innumerable methods of deliverance unknown to us lie in his power, we conceive of him as a dead idol. Keil and Delitzsch supply the grammar: the clause about the sanctuary is the apodosis, so that acknowledging him as the Holy One is what makes him one.
14:
Calvin builds the promise on a pun the English loses. The word for sanctuary shares a root with the verb to sanctify just before, so that God demands nothing for which he offers no recompense: whoever sanctifies him will find him a sanctuary. He marks the difference within it, since we sanctify him by ascribing all glory to him, while he sanctifies us by guarding us from evils. The sanctuary he pictures as a citadel on a height, defending the godly and destroying the ungodly who run against it.

Gill rejects the reading that makes the sanctuary the invading king, which he ascribes to Aben Ezra, and follows the Targum in taking it of the Word of the Lord, adding that the Septuagint renders it sanctification. Ellicott translates it as a hallowed thing and carries over the sense in which a sanctuary was also an asylum. Wesley makes it a sure refuge for all who truly fear God. Clarke finds the text defective. He judges the words unto you necessary to the sense and lost here, though preserved in the Vulgate, while the Septuagint has the singular, it shall be to thee. Failing that we should have to read snare for sanctuary, pointlessly repeated at the end of the verse; the Chaldee reads judgment. He settles for the Vulgate as the best remedy.

Ellicott supplies the link the two halves need. To enter fellowship with God is to enter the sanctuary, and the man standing on its threshold stone has gained his asylum; but that requires the clear vision of faith, so a man walking blindly may stumble on that same stone, and what was life to others brings him pain and shame, leaving him bruised like an animal in a trap until a helper releases him. He also insists the fall is not necessarily final: men may be bruised without being ground to powder, and may stumble so as to rise again.

The naming of both houses provokes a quarrel. Calvin reports that the Jewish interpreters tear the verse asunder instead of dividing it, saying God will be partly a sanctuary and partly a stone, as though the two families distinguished the godly from the unbelievers. He denies it: the prophet names both kingdoms because he means the whole nation, and then names the capital as a further heightening, since even there, where God seemed to keep his abode, he would be a stone. Wesley keeps the two kingdoms as the plain sense. Ellicott reads the peculiar phrase as implying a hope of the restored unity of the national life.

Calvin sees the words fulfilled partly under Hezekiah and partly at the captivity, and holds that Christ was prefigured in them; and he warns that it is no new thing for a great multitude who boast that they belong to the Church to be alienated from the God whose name they carry, so the few should hold to him however small their number.

On the piling up of verbs in the last verse Ellicott suggests each carried a distinct force now only partly recoverable, and that read against the trap of the previous verse they give the stages of a capture: the animal stumbles, falls into the pit, breaks its limbs, is fastened, and cannot escape. Calvin reads the sequence as a threat that those refusing to trust God will not go unpunished, and should not imagine themselves stronger or wiser than he is. He adds that the threat serves the godly too; and is careful to say that this destroying office does not strictly belong to God, whose proper work is to receive men into favour, but is accidental, so the stumbling of unbelievers need not obstruct anyone faith. Gill and Wesley both hold the limit in the word many: not all, since a remnant was foretold, and the stone was set for rising as well as falling.
16:
Gill settles the speaker: these are not the prophet words, as Kimchi thought, but the words of the Lord to him, and Ellicott agrees that God speaks. Ellicott takes the disciples to be those who looked to the prophet as guide, and explains the actions from practice: the words go on a parchment roll, as men wrote the book of the law, and it is sealed partly against tampering, partly as an attestation, like the seal on a royal letter, that it was authentic. Wesley reads the imperatives prophetically, as a direction to declare that the thing shall be bound and sealed, both words designing one thing, security and secrecy, so that it should be fulfilled and yet kept hidden from the unbelieving. Both take the two nouns of any revelation of God.

Calvin turns the whole into the figure of a letter. Many may handle it, but only the addressee reads it; so the word is held out to all and received by few, unsealed to his own by the Spirit. He defends the rendering bind against those who derive the verb from another root, since the ancient custom was to tie a thread round a letter before sealing it. From this comes the encouragement he thinks the passage exists to give: ministers must persevere though all men appear to revolt, for the Lord will reserve some disciples by whom the letter is read with profit while it stays closed to others. He denies that the prophet was to shut himself up with his few, since God still willed him to cry aloud.

Henry treats the passage as privilege. It is a great instance of the care of God for his Church that he has lodged in it the treasure of divine revelation, a testimony directing faith and a law directing practice. He reads the sealing as a bar against adding or diminishing; and takes the binding of the older testimony to mean that the full explication of many prophecies was reserved for later times, so what was sealed is now open, though it stays bound as to the world to come, since we know only in part.

Clarke adds a note of another kind. The Septuagint rendered the phrase about the disciples in a way suggesting a different word, meaning that it be not understood; Bishop Chandler approved that reading, which Clarke has from Archbishop Secker.

At the turn to the prophet own resolve Calvin renders the particle as yet: since God is pleased to have disciples to whom the doctrine is sealed, I will wait for him though he hide his face. He calls this the only remedy left, and names what makes the trial hard, that faith is shaken worst when we find ourselves stripped of allies and see open enemies boldly taking the name of the Church. Wesley reads the same yet against the dreadful prophecy just uttered, making the waiting an expectation of the Messiah, as Gill does.

Keil and Delitzsch treat what precedes as the prophet own prayer, offered while he waits; the judgment now begun would last long, but the word of God was the pledge of the continuance of the nation, so he hopes for the grace hidden behind the wrath. Ellicott notes that the verse comes in abruptly, but not enough to justify the assumption of some critics that a verse has been lost. He reads it as precept enforced by example, the prophet having conquered the feverish desire to know the future that drove men to soothsayers, from which even his own disciples were not exempt; and finds a contrast in it, since all is dark for the national life while the prophet in his own person can still look for him with the eye of faith. Henry sets the point plainest: the prophet foresaw the hiding of the face and yet looked for a return of favour.
18:
Who speaks here is the sharpest division in the chapter. Gill takes the words as those of Christ presenting himself and his spiritual offspring, not the prophet speaking of his own sons or disciples. Wesley holds them spoken literally by the prophet and mystically of Christ. Calvin keeps the prophet as speaker and reads the gesture as courage: though others withdraw, he comes forward with those God preserved through him, promising to persevere though all revolt. Ellicott takes them of the prophet, finding in his own name and his sons a revelation of the future; and adds a blunt judgment about the quotation, that it shows how little the writer of that epistle cared for the original sense, enough for him being that Christ, like the prophet, was not alone. Keil and Delitzsch call the act a presentation, the children being a gift for a higher purpose than family enjoyment.

What the signs are is disputed too. Keil and Delitzsch make the first an omen pledging something future, the second a marvel pointing back to a supernatural cause or a type pointing beyond itself, the word meaning twisted round, out of the ordinary course. Calvin rejects that line: some refer the passage to miracles, but the meaning is that the godly are looked on with abhorrence as monsters, not only by strangers but by their own countrymen. Wesley puts it colloquially, a gazing flock for the folly of believing the promises of God. Clarke notes only that one manuscript reads God of hosts for Lord of hosts.

On the children as a gift Calvin builds a doctrine of teaching, adding that teachers must bring disciples with them rather than send them ahead. Faith is to be ascribed to God and his election, since the prophet invited everyone and profited only those given him, whom God drew inwardly while the outward voice fell on the crowd without effect.

The temptation that follows is one Ellicott thinks the disciples all but yielded to: why not consult the soothsayers so much in demand about the secrets of coming years? He calls the English phrase for the spirit consulted a happy paraphrase rather than a translation, and connects it with necromancy as in the story of the witch of Endor. Keil and Delitzsch supply the setting: heathen superstition had reached the capital and was practised as a trade, and the answer is put into the mouths of the children and disciples.

The answer divides Calvin from the others. It is commonly expounded, he says, as an argument from less to greater: the nations consult their gods, false as they are, so shall we not more esteem the true God? Wesley gives that reading. Calvin refuses it and applies the words to the Jews themselves, called a people by eminence because God had adopted them, defending the point from the grammar of the pronoun. He treats the sentence as a shield against superstitions that creep in unnoticed: while men ponder whether to consult diviners, the answer is that God alone is to be consulted, having willed to be their teacher and appointed prophets for it. Clarke reports that the Septuagint repeat the verb, yielding a second question about seeking to the dead concerning the living, thinks the repetition necessary, and adds from Procopius that it expresses the indignation of the prophet at their folly. Ellicott finds the last clause abruptly elliptical and turns it into questions of his own: what ground is there for thinking the dead can be recalled, or that they know more than the living, and might they not know less? He takes the state of the departed to be not annihilation but dormant power. Wesley keeps it simpler, that for living men to enquire of the living God is reasonable, and that to forsake him for dead idols, whether images or the spirits supposed to speak in them, is highly absurd.
20:
The appeal to the law is first a question of grammar. Gill reports that Kimchi read it as an oath, by the law and by the testimony, and that Aben Ezra objected there is no such formula in Scripture. Calvin rejects it on the preposition, which directs attention to the law rather than swearing by it, and treats testimony as a description of the law. Whatever men introduce on their own authority, he adds, is a corruption of the word. Ellicott takes law and testimony as the word given to the prophet himself, denying they are more than remotely an exhortation to study Scripture.

What the last clause means divides them four ways. Wesley refers it to the antagonists, whose want of light comes from the darkness of their own minds. Keil and Delitzsch render it that they are a people for whom no morning dawns, treat the summons as a battle watchword, and read the particle conditionally against Knobel, who takes it as a question, and Luzzatto, who takes it as an oath. Ellicott renders for them there is no light of morning, meaning hope rather than knowledge, so that no dawn shines on men who haunt the darkened rooms of the diviners. Clarke, who has from Archbishop Secker the suggestion that the two terms point back to the attested prophecy at the head of the chapter, denies that morning is the sense at all. The word serves elsewhere as an adjective for dark and a noun for gloom, and rendering it morning yields no meaning; the clause should say that in the word there is no obscurity. Calvin reads it as encouragement: wicked men who leave the true doctrine show only their own blindness.

Gill marks the punishment as beginning at the next verse, taking the unnamed place to be the land, after the Targum and Kimchi. Calvin presses the verb, which describes men wandering without a resting place, against the promise of a fixed inheritance. Ellicott reports that the abruptness of the opening has led critics such as Cheyne to transpose the two verses, and suspects the hunger is as figurative as the darkness, a famine not of bread but of hearing the word of the Lord; the faithful might bear both as soldiers bear a night march, while the panicked crowd turns to cursing.

What they curse is disputed. Ellicott takes both objects literally, the king who led them to destruction and the God they had neglected, declining the reading that makes the two one. Wesley agrees on the king, but takes the second of their idol. Calvin distinguishes the two, since their boasting had been partly in idols and partly in their king, so they are brought to abhor both; and treats the loathing as possibly the beginning of repentance, though in the reprobate the same bitterness only aggravates their rage. On the upward look Ellicott is firm that it means despair and defiance rather than hope, since on every side there is nothing but darkness, so that like Dante they find themselves where the sun is silent.

Clarke ends with two notes. On the word rendered hardly bestead he prefers the reading of the Vulgate, the Chaldee and Symmachus, tottering through weakness. He also reports from Michaelis a passage in the Koran built on the same figure, of travellers who walk while the lightning flashes and stand still when it fails, with the story of Labid, one of the seven Arabian poets whose verses hung at Mecca, who judged that no man could have written it without inspiration. Calvin closes on the aggravation: darkness and trouble are the usual figures for adversity, and a man already in the dark who is driven further in is in more danger of stumbling. Wesley puts the despair in a sentence: finding no help from heaven, they turn their eyes downward for comfort.
